key_insight: Polystyrene can intensify initial shock-induced heating at HMX pore interfaces, yet its subsequent heat-absorbing reactions suppress hotspot growth and coalescence.
engineering_relevance: Explosive safety and initiation models should account for binder chemistry as well as pore geometry because early hotspot heating does not necessarily predict sustained reaction growth.
method: Reactive molecular dynamics of shock-driven void collapse in an HMX crystal–gap–crystal stack.
Polystyrene placed along the upstream crystal surface.
Characterization of void-length effects, hotspot evolution, and polymer reactions.
evidence_signal: The simulations show void-length dependence in pressure–volume work, shock temperature, and self-sustaining chemistry onset, while polymer chain scission and extensive aromatic–backbone cross-bonding absorb heat and inhibit hotspot growth.
watch_item: The abstract reports simulation evidence for a specific HMX–polystyrene geometry, so transferability to other binders and realistic pore networks requires validation.
paper_title: Polymer-Mediated Hotspot Evolution in Shock-Induced Pore Collapse in 1,3,5,7-Tetranitro-1,3,5,7-tetrazocane (HMX)-based Explosives
